Empirical Research Plan ‑ “How Does an Extra Child Affect Parental Labour Supply?”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Two–Stage Least Squares (IV).

Why IV is appropriate  
•  Endogenous regressor: family size (having ≥3 vs. exactly 2 children) is jointly chosen with labour-supply.  
•  Exogenous sources of variation are available:  
  1. Same-sex vs. mixed-sex of the first two children (“SameSex12”).  
  2. Twin birth at the second pregnancy (“Twin2”).  
Given biological randomness of child sex and (pre-IVF) twinning, these variables satisfy relevance and, plausibly, exogeneity.  
•  The data are essentially cross-sectional (1980 & 1990 censuses), so panel DID/Event-study designs are infeasible; RDD does not fit because there is no running variable with a policy cutoff.

We therefore estimate labour-supply outcome Y on the endogenous dummy  3+Kids  using SameSex12 (baseline) and Twin2 (robustness) as instruments, controlling for rich covariates and fixed effects.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------
•  Treatment variable D (endogenous):  
   D = 1 if the mother has three or more children, 0 if exactly two children.

•  Instruments Z  
   Z1 = 1 if the first two children are the same sex; 0 otherwise.  
   Z2 = 1 if the second birth is a multiple birth; 0 otherwise.

•  Control/comparison group: mothers with exactly two children (D = 0).  
   Fathers married to these mothers form the analogous sample for paternal outcomes.

•  Timing: We observe outcomes at the census date. Because the oldest child is <18 and the mother is 21-35, parity decisions and subsequent labour-supply have already been realised.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------
A1  Relevance: SameSex12 and Twin2 must increase the probability of having ≥3 children.  
— Highly plausible and well-documented empirically (check 1st-stage F-stats).

A2  Independence (quasi-random assignment): conditional on controls, SameSex12 and Twin2 are independent of unobserved determinants of parental labour supply.  
— Sex of a child is biologically random; twinning is essentially random in this period. We restrict to pre-IVF years (≤1990) and singleton first births to bolster plausibility.

A3  Exclusion: Instruments affect labour-supply only through their impact on family size.  
— Potential threats: (i) caring for boys vs. girls may directly affect time use; (ii) twins may impose extra physical/health shocks. We probe these in Section 4.

A4  Monotonicity: No parents reduce family size because of the instrument (e.g., no one aborts a pregnancy when the first two children are same-sex).  
— Reasonable given U.S. norms and legal environment.

A5  SUTVA: One family’s fertility “treatment” does not affect another’s labour-supply.  
— Plausible in individual-level census data.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
-------------------------------------------------
T1  Direct gender-composition effects (violates exclusion).  
   •  Address by:  
     – Including dummies for the actual sex of 1st and 2nd child (BoyGirl, GirlBoy, etc.) so only the same-sex indicator’s variation remains.  
     – Running placebo tests on families with only two children; SameSex12 should have no effect on their labour supply.

T2  Non-random twinning due to fertility treatment or maternal age.  
   •  Mitigation:  
     – Restrict to 2nd births in 1980 Census when IVF was negligible.  
     – Control flexibly for mother’s age and race (twins more common among older, Black, and tall mothers).  
     – Show covariate balance between Twin2=1 and Twin2=0.

T3  Selection into the sample (both parents present, oldest child <18, etc.).  
   •  Test robustness to varying the age window (e.g., mothers 25-40), include single mothers in separate analyses, and document attrition patterns.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------- 0. Packages ----------
library(data.table)   # fast I/O
library(fixest)       # IV regressions & FEs
library(estimatr)     # for robust SEs
library(sandwich)
library(modelsummary)

# ---------- 1. Load Data ----------
pums80  <- fread("PUMS_1980.csv")
pums90  <- fread("PUMS_1990.csv")
pums    <- rbindlist(list(pums80, pums90), fill = TRUE)

# ---------- 2. Sample Selection ----------
pums <- pums[
  SEX == "Female" & MARST == "Married, spouse present" &
  AGE >= 21 & AGE <= 35 &
  OLDEST_CHILD_AGE < 18 &
  CHILDREN_EVER_BORN >= 2
]

# ---------- 3. Variable Construction ----------
pums[, `:=`(
  three_plus      = as.integer(CHILDREN_EVER_BORN >= 3),
  same_sex_12     = as.integer(SEX_CHILD1 == SEX_CHILD2),
  twin2           = as.integer(BIRTH2_PLURALITY > 1),       # 1=multiple
  ln_earnings     = log(pmax(EARNINGS, 1)),                 # avoid log(0)
  employed        = as.integer(WEEKS_WORKED > 0),
  hours_worked    = HOURS_PER_WEEK,
  weeks_worked    = WEEKS_WORKED,
  year            = factor(YEAR),
  state           = factor(STATEFIP),
  age_fe          = factor(AGE),
  race_fe         = factor(RACED)
)]

# Fathers’ file can be constructed analogously by linking spouse IDs.

# ---------- 4. Main 2SLS ----------
spec_base <- feols(
  employed ~ three_plus | same_sex_12 ~ age_fe + race_fe + education + state + year,
  data = pums, cluster = ~state
)
summary(spec_base, stage = 2)   # returns 1st & 2nd stage

# ---------- 5. Alternative Instrument (Twins) ----------
spec_twin <- feols(
  employed ~ three_plus | twin2 ~ age_fe + race_fe + education + state + year,
  data = pums, cluster = ~state
)

# ---------- 6. Robustness – placebo on 2-kid families ----------
placebo <- feols(
  employed ~ same_sex_12 + age_fe + race_fe + education + state + year,
  data = pums[three_plus == 0], cluster = ~state
)

# ---------- 7. Output ----------
modelsummary(list(Base = spec_base, Twin = spec_twin, Placebo = placebo),
             estimate = "{estimate} ({std.error})",
             gof_omit = ".*")
```

Notes  
• `feols(y ~ d | z ~ controls)` is the fixest syntax for 2SLS with cluster-robust SEs.  
• Additional outcomes (`hours_worked`, `weeks_worked`, `ln_earnings`) are run identically.  
• Balance tests: regress each pre-determined characteristic on the instruments.

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts an additional child raises home-production demands, lowering mothers’ labour-supply; fathers’ supply may rise slightly or stay flat.

Ball-park priors (mothers):  
• Employment probability ↓ 8–12 pp (roughly a 15–20 % reduction from a 60 % baseline).  
• Annual hours ↓ ~200–250 (≈ 7 %), driven mainly by weeks worked.  
• Labour earnings ↓ 6–10 %.  

Fathers: effects close to zero or small positive (≤3 pp).

Heterogeneity: larger negative effects for unmarried and less-educated women.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
-------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10)  …… 1  
C2: Instrument exogeneity (balance on observables)  …… 0.8  
C3: Exclusion restriction credible  …… 0.6  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers)  …… 0.9  
C5: Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers)  …… 1  

Average score ≈ 0.86 — reasonably strong but exclusion remains the main concern.
